issues.legal_issue: The revisional authority retains jurisdiction over an order made under a repealed enactment when successive deeming provisions treat that order as made under the replacement enactment.
material_facts: A subordinate authority declared property to be evacuee property under an earlier ordinance.
Successive enactments provided that things done under the repealed enactment were to be treated as done under the succeeding enactment, including the replacement Act.
The replacement Act conferred revisional power on the Custodian-General, and the earlier ordinance had declared the subordinate authority’s order final.
The State later invoked the Custodian-General’s revisional jurisdiction to challenge the declaration.
issues.conclusion: The Custodian-General had jurisdiction to entertain the revision; the earlier order’s finality under the repealed ordinance did not prevent the replacement Act’s revisional power from applying to it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, read with the transitional deeming provision in section 55(3) of Ordinance 27 of 1949, carried forward the earlier order as one made under the replacement Act. The saving of the previous operation of the repealed law did not preserve its future operation or override the revisional jurisdiction conferred by section 27 of the Act. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 applies only where a different intention does not appear; section 58(3) expressed a different intention. The Court explained Indira Sohanlal v. Custodian of Evacuee Property and distinguished the relevant observations in Dafadar Niranjan Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, where the chain of deeming provisions had been broken.

rule.if: revision_jurisdiction_dispute and earlier_order_under_repealed_law and successive_deeming_provisions_apply and replacement_law_confers_revision

predicates.revision_jurisdiction_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a revisional authority may review an order made by a subordinate authority.
predicates.earlier_order_under_repealed_law: A subordinate authority made the challenged order under an enactment that was later repealed.
predicates.successive_deeming_provisions_apply: Successive enactments treat acts done under each repealed enactment as acts done under the succeeding enactment.
predicates.replacement_law_confers_revision: The enactment treated as governing the earlier order gives a designated authority power to revise subordinate orders.

issues.definition: When a revision-jurisdiction dispute concerns an earlier order carried through successive deeming provisions into a law that confers revision power, the revisional authority has jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional decision based on new documentary evidence cannot stand when the affected party is denied a fair opportunity to meet that evidence.
material_facts: The State relied on copies of documents to support its claim to the property, and the Custodian-General relied on those documents in reaching the decision.
The documents were introduced in the revision proceeding, and the originals were not produced there.
The affected parties were not told that the copies had been admitted and were not given an opportunity to inspect the documents or present evidence in rejoinder.
The Custodian-General set aside the earlier order on the basis of the State’s case.
issues.conclusion: The procedure violated natural justice; the Custodian-General’s order was set aside and the matter was remanded for the documents to be formally tendered and both sides to have an opportunity to present evidence and submissions.
issues.legal_principle: The rules of natural justice require a fair opportunity to answer evidence relied on against a party. Under rule 31(9) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Central Rules, 1950, the revisional authority may admit additional evidence in an appropriate case, but a party has no right to have additional evidence admitted. The authority must decide whether to admit it in the interests of justice, and an affected party must be allowed to meet evidence that is admitted and relied on.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A revisional authority is deciding whether to disturb an earlier order.
predicates.new_evidence_relied_on: A party presents evidence not previously on the record, and the revisional authority relies on it in deciding the matter.
predicates.affected_party_denied_opportunity_to_ans: The party affected by the new evidence is not given a fair chance to inspect, rebut, or respond to it.

issues.definition: If a revisional authority relies on new evidence without giving the affected party a fair chance to answer it, the resulting order is set aside and the matter is remanded.

issues.legal_issue: Substantial delay in seeking revision does not by itself require the Supreme Court to disturb the revisional authority’s discretionary decision to entertain the proceeding when no statutory time limit applies.
material_facts: The State sought revision many years after the challenged order, although proceedings concerning the property had occurred in the interim and the interests of purchasers had intervened.
The Court considered that the State’s authorities appeared grossly negligent in protecting the asserted public interest.
The Custodian-General exercised the view that the revision should nevertheless be entertained.
The appeal challenged that exercise of discretion.
issues.conclusion: Whether to entertain a substantially delayed revision was within the Custodian-General’s discretion, and the Supreme Court would not interfere with that decision in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 authorises revision at any time and prescribes no limitation period. The revisional power is judicial, and delay, particularly where other persons’ titles have intervened, may bear on whether the authority should exercise its discretion. The Supreme Court declined to interfere under Article 136 of the Constitution with the authority’s discretionary decision on that matter.

predicates.appeal_from_revision_decision: The proceeding before the Supreme Court challenges a decision made by a revisional authority.
predicates.revision_power_has_no_time_limit: The law granting revision power sets no time limit for its exercise.
predicates.authority_entertained_revision_despite_s: The revisional authority chose to hear a revision brought after a substantial delay.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a decision to entertain a substantially delayed revision under a power with no time limit, the Supreme Court does not disturb that discretionary choice.
